The tandem bicycle had two saddles and two sets of pedals. I chose the rear saddle because it looked higher. Only after Aunt Mina started down the lane did I discover that my handlebar did not steer.
"What is it for, then?" I asked.
"Holding on."
Hers decided every turn. Mine stayed stubbornly in place, a very convincing imitation of something important. I began to feel like an extra suitcase with knees.
"I seem to be ornamental," I announced.
Aunt Mina did not answer. Ahead of us, the lane climbed toward a stone bridge. Her shoulders bent forward, and the easy rhythm of our pedals slowed.
"A little more help back there?" she called.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why can crushing sugar speed its dissolving?

choices.A: It exposes more sugar surface to the water.
choices.B: It increases the quantity of water.
choices.C: It automatically raises the water’s temperature.
choices.D: It changes sugar into a different substance.

questions.correctAnswer: It exposes more sugar surface to the water.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies increased exposed surface as the reason water can contact more sugar at once.
questions.stimulusText:
A confectioner preparing syrup may crush sugar to help it dissolve quickly. Crushing exposes more surface to the water. Water can then reach more of the sugar at once, so small grains generally disappear faster than an equal mass in a large lump under otherwise similar conditions.
Speed, however, is not the same as the amount that can dissolve. For a given quantity of water at a fixed temperature, there is a limit to how much sugar can remain dissolved. Crushing does not by itself raise that limit. If the water has already reached it, adding powdered sugar will not make the extra sugar stay dissolved simply because its grains are small.
A solution at this limit is described as saturated. With excess sugar present, some solid remains after sufficient time, whether that excess began as powder or as large crystals. The solid might be harder to notice when its pieces are tiny, but invisibility at a glance is not proof that everything has dissolved.
The confectioner therefore asks two different questions: How soon must the syrup be ready, and how much sugar must it contain? Grain size can help answer the first. The second requires attention to the amount of water and its temperature. Confusing the questions can produce a faster process without the intended result.

questions.stimulusTitle: Where a Monument Places the Visitor
questions.stimulusText:
Imagine two proposed monuments remembering the same voyage. Each design uses the same kind and quantity of stone. In one, a tall figure stands on a high pedestal, looking toward the horizon. In the other, the travelers' names run along a low wall, where visitors can stand close enough to trace individual letters.
The first design places the visitor below a commanding image. The upward gaze and distant horizon can emphasize determination, leadership, or an achievement viewed as a single dramatic act. The second distributes attention across many names. Visitors may move slowly along the wall, looking for a relative or noticing a name they have never heard.
These differences are not merely matters of decoration. Height, distance, and arrangement invite different kinds of attention. The stone is a kind of script for the visitor's movement, though nobody is forced to follow it exactly.
Nor does either design dictate one inevitable emotion. A visitor might admire the tall figure, question whom it represents, or simply study the carving. Someone at the wall might feel connection, curiosity, or uncertainty. Design can guide an encounter without controlling every response.
Comparing the proposals therefore requires more than asking which uses finer stone. We should ask what each makes prominent, whose presence it records, and how it positions the people who come to remember.

questions.stimulusText:
Uncle Davin gave me an umbrella with tiny foxes painted inside its canopy. "Something better than clouds to look at," he said.
I decided it deserved a special occasion. A walk to the vegetable market did not qualify, but I brought it along because leaving it at home seemed ungrateful.
Halfway there, the rain began. I tucked the folded umbrella under my coat. The canopy remained pristine; I was not faring as well. Water ran from my hair into my collar, and the shopping list softened in my pocket.
At the market, the woman selling potatoes looked at my dripping sleeves.
"Doesn't it open?" she asked.
"Of course. It was a present."
"Ah," she said. "I thought it was an umbrella."
I examined the neat dry folds. Uncle Davin had spent an evening painting foxes that I had seen only once, when he first opened the canopy. Since then, I had protected them so successfully that they might as well have stayed in a cupboard.
I stepped away from the stall and pressed the catch. Above me, the foxes appeared among green leaves. Drops pattered on the other side, where they belonged.
The woman handed me the potatoes. "A suitable occasion?"
"An excellent one," I said, and walked home beneath my present.

questions.prompt: Which term names the attraction between water and the glass surface?

choices.A: Cohesion
choices.B: Gravity
choices.C: Evaporation
choices.D: Adhesion

questions.correctAnswer: Adhesion
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly labels the water–glass attraction adhesion and distinguishes it from water molecules attracting one another.
questions.stimulusText:
Place the lower end of a clean, narrow glass tube in water, and water can rise inside it above the level outside. No pump is hidden in the tube. The effect involves interactions among the water, the glass, and gravity.
Water is attracted to the glass surface, an interaction called adhesion. Water molecules also attract one another; this is cohesion. Near the glass, these interactions help produce a curved water surface. The forces at that surface can support a small column of water against its weight.
The rising column becomes heavier as it grows taller. Eventually, its weight balances the upward supporting effect, and the rise stops. Thus, the observation does not show that gravity has disappeared or that water can climb to any height.
Under comparable conditions with water and clean glass, a narrower tube supports a higher rise than a wider one. The narrower column has less water to support relative to the amount of contact around its edge.
Similar effects help water spread through the narrow spaces in a paper towel. Those spaces form passages among fibers; the water does not need to flow through the solid material of each fiber. When spreading occurs horizontally, it need not lift an increasingly tall column against gravity. One mechanism can therefore appear in different arrangements, whose limits depend partly on their geometry.

questions.prompt: In this bell, what movement opens the circuit?

choices.A: The button is released after every strike.
choices.B: The moving arm separates the contact surfaces.
choices.C: The spring removes the coil from the bell.
choices.D: The electrical source changes into a magnet.

questions.correctAnswer: The moving arm separates the contact surfaces.
questions.explanation: The arm’s movement both carries the striker toward the bell and separates the contact surfaces, interrupting current through the coil.
questions.stimulusText:
In one simple electric bell, holding down a button produces a rapid series of strikes. Yet current does not flow continuously through the bell's electromagnet. A moving contact repeatedly interrupts it.
When the button is held and the contact is closed, current flows through a coil. The coil acts as an electromagnet and pulls a spring-mounted metal arm toward it. A striker attached to the arm hits the bell. That same movement separates the contact surfaces, opening the circuit.
The broken circuit stops current through the coil, so the magnetic pull disappears. The spring then returns the arm toward its starting position. This closes the contact again. With the button still held, current can resume, the electromagnet pulls again, and the cycle repeats.
The interruption is therefore part of normal operation, rather than evidence that the bell has failed. If the arm were held against the electromagnet and the circuit stayed closed, the repeated release-and-return motion would not occur in the described way.
Nor does the bell create its own supply of energy. An electrical source provides energy during the connected portions of the cycle. The spring helps return the arm, but it does not replace that source. The design makes one sustained request at the button produce many brief electrical and mechanical events inside the bell.

questions.prompt: What starting condition allows the two spoons to have the same initial temperature in the passage?

choices.A: One has just been removed from an oven.
choices.B: The wooden spoon is twice as long.
choices.C: They have remained in the same room long enough.
choices.D: Both have been held in a hand continuously.

questions.correctAnswer: They have remained in the same room long enough.
questions.explanation: The opening specifies that the spoons have been left in the same room long enough, establishing the equal-temperature starting condition.
questions.stimulusText:
A metal spoon and a wooden spoon left in the same room long enough can begin at the same temperature. Touch them with a warm hand, however, and the metal may feel colder. The sensation does not by itself establish that the metal started colder.
When the hand is warmer than the spoon, energy moves from the skin into the object. Metal generally conducts heat away from the contact region more readily than wood does. It can therefore keep drawing energy from the touching skin quickly, cooling that small region of skin more rapidly.
Wood transfers heat through itself more slowly. Its contact region warms sooner and limits further rapid heat loss from the skin. The hand consequently experiences a different rate of cooling, even though the two objects began at the same temperature.
This is a comparison of heat transfer, not a claim that metal is always colder than wood. If both objects start hotter than the skin, the direction of transfer reverses. The more rapid transfer can then make the metal feel hotter instead.
A thermometer and a hand are thus answering different questions. A suitable thermometer can compare the objects' initial temperatures. The hand registers the effect of their interaction with the skin, including how quickly energy moves. Feeling colder and having a lower initial temperature are related possibilities, but they are not interchangeable descriptions.

questions.stimulusText:
A metal spoon and a wooden spoon left in the same room long enough can begin at the same temperature. Touch them with a warm hand, however, and the metal may feel colder. The sensation does not by itself establish that the metal started colder.
When the hand is warmer than the spoon, energy moves from the skin into the object. Metal generally conducts heat away from the contact region more readily than wood does. It can therefore keep drawing energy from the touching skin quickly, cooling that small region of skin more rapidly.
Wood transfers heat through itself more slowly. Its contact region warms sooner and limits further rapid heat loss from the skin. The hand consequently experiences a different rate of cooling, even though the two objects began at the same temperature.
This is a comparison of heat transfer, not a claim that metal is always colder than wood. If both objects start hotter than the skin, the direction of transfer reverses. The more rapid transfer can then make the metal feel hotter instead.
A thermometer and a hand are thus answering different questions. A suitable thermometer can compare the objects' initial temperatures. The hand registers the effect of their interaction with the skin, including how quickly energy moves. Feeling colder and having a lower initial temperature are related possibilities, but they are not interchangeable descriptions.

questions.stimulusTitle: A Street Built for One View
questions.stimulusText:
Imagine a theater set that suggests a long street within a shallow stage. The doorway nearest the audience is nearly full size. Successive doorways are smaller, and the gaps between them shrink. Floor lines narrow toward a point farther back. From a chosen viewing position, these changes can make the street seem to extend much farther than it physically does.
The design borrows expectations from ordinary seeing. Distant buildings appear smaller, and parallel road edges seem to approach one another. The set exaggerates and arranges those cues within a restricted space. Its apparent depth is constructed from relationships among the forms, not from a hidden stretch of actual street.
This illusion depends partly on where the observer sits. From far to one side, edges that align from the intended position may separate, exposing the arrangement. The stage street is foreshortened: its physical depth is compressed in order to suggest a greater depth from that selected view.
An audience can understand this construction without losing all pleasure in it. Watching a play does not require believing that a real town has been fitted behind the curtain. The painted and built forms serve a dramatic purpose. Judging them only by the standards of a street that people must use every day would miss the particular achievement: making a limited space support a convincing imagined one.
